scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `adaptyv` skill is a documentation-only skill describing the Adaptyv Bio Foundry REST API and Python SDK. It contains no script files, no obfuscated content, no network exfiltration logic, and no prompt-injection, jailbreak, or concealment directives. The bundled reference file (`references/api-endpoints.md`) is a straightforward endpoint reference consistent with the stated purpose. Credential guidance is sound (environment variables / .env, explicit 'never hardcode' and 'never commit' warnings). The declared `allowed-tools` (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the described behavior of writing API client code and running install/curl commands. Only minor issues were identified: an unpinned GitHub dependency install, a documented auto-accept-quote automation pattern with billing implications, guidance to read .env files, and three referenced files that are not present in the package. Overall risk is LOW; the skill appears benign and its description matches its behavior.
llm_primary_threats: Automated financial commitment pattern without user confirmation

findings.title: Instruction to locate and load project .env files
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to check the project root for a `.env` file and load it to obtain the API token. While this is a common and generally safe credential-handling practice (and the skill explicitly forbids hardcoding or committing tokens), it does direct the agent to read files that commonly contain unrelated secrets, which could surface those secrets in the conversation context.
findings.snippet: Check for a `.env` file in the project root first; if one exists, use a library like `python-dotenv` to load it.
findings.remediation: Scope the guidance to reading only the `ADAPTYV_API_KEY` variable and instruct the agent never to echo or log the contents of `.env` files.

findings.title: Documented automation pattern that bypasses human review of billing commitments
findings.description: The skill documents an 'Automated Pipeline' example that sets `skip_draft: True` and `auto_accept_quote: True`, which bypasses the Draft state and automatically accepts a vendor quote and creates a Stripe invoice. If an agent copies this pattern verbatim, the user could incur real financial charges without explicit confirmation. This is a legitimate upstream API feature, but the skill presents it without a caution to confirm with the user first.
findings.snippet:
"skip_draft": True,
    "auto_accept_quote": True,
findings.remediation: Add an explicit instruction that the agent must obtain user confirmation before using `auto_accept_quote`/`skip_draft`, since these create binding financial commitments.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installed directly from GitHub
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to install the `adaptyv-sdk` package directly from a GitHub repository without pinning a commit, tag, or version (`uv pip install "git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"`). Any change to the default branch of that repository (including a compromise of the upstream account) would be executed on the user's machine at install time. The repository appears to be the legitimate vendor org and the package is documented as not yet on PyPI, so the risk is limited, but provenance is unverified.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
uv add "adaptyv-sdk @ git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
findings.remediation: Pin the install to a specific tag or commit hash (e.g., `git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git@<commit-sha>`) and advise the user to review the repository before installation.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The admet-prediction skill is a domain-specific cheminformatics helper and appears benign. Both bundled Python scripts (admet_batch.py, admet_report.py) use only the Python standard library (argparse, csv, json, pathlib, sys), perform no network I/O, spawn no subprocesses, and contain no eval/exec, obfuscation, encoded payloads, or credential access. File reads/writes are limited to user-specified input CSV/SMILES files and an explicitly named output directory, consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). The SKILL.md body and the two reference documents contain no prompt-injection, role-override, concealment, or safety-bypass language; they are scientific guidance that in fact encourages conservative interpretation and human verification. The description includes a list of trigger keywords (ADMET-AI, hERG, CYP3A4, Caco-2, etc.), but these are narrowly scoped and directly relevant to the skill's stated function, so they do not constitute capability inflation or keyword baiting. Several referenced paths under assets/ and templates/ were not found, but the actual references/ files exist and are benign; the missing paths are documentation artifacts, not security issues. Only a minor supply-chain note (unpinned pip install with remote model weight download) is worth flagging.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instruction
findings.description: Documentation instructs the user to run `pip install admet-ai` without a pinned version (the SKILL.md mentions 'admet-ai 2.0+'). The package also downloads model weights from the network on first use. This is standard practice for scientific tooling and the referenced repository (swansonk14/admet_ai) is a well-known MIT-licensed project, but unpinned installs plus remote weight download introduce a minor supply-chain consideration.
findings.snippet:
```bash
pip install admet-ai
```
... "Model weights download on first use."
findings.remediation: Pin an exact version (e.g., `pip install admet-ai==2.0.1`) and document the expected model weight source/checksums.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The antibody-engineering skill is a self-contained, benign scientific tooling package. All three Python scripts (number_antibody.py, scan_liabilities.py, physchem_profile.py) use only the standard library (argparse, csv, re, sys, pathlib) plus an optional, clearly declared third-party dependency (anarci) that is imported defensively and never installed automatically. There is no network activity, no subprocess or shell execution, no eval/exec, no dynamic imports, no base64 or other obfuscation, no environment-variable or credential access, and no hardcoded secrets. File I/O is limited to user-supplied FASTA/CSV/TSV inputs and an explicit --out path, which is consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language in any language; it is plain domain documentation and in fact urges conservative interpretation of results ('a liability is a question, not a veto', 'say no sequence liabilities detected, structure-based properties not assessed'). The bundled reference documents are ordinary technical notes with no embedded instructions to the agent. Cross-component consistency is good: the description accurately reflects what the scripts do. Only two LOW informational observations were recorded.

findings.title: Activation keyword list appended to description

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The ncats-arax skill is a documentation-only package (no executable scripts included) describing a tightly constrained CLI client for the public NCATS Translator ARAX biomedical knowledge-graph API. The SKILL.md body and both reference files contain no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, safety-bypass language, obfuscation, or credential access. The declared scope (Read, Bash to invoke a bundled Python client; outbound HTTPS to a single named public research endpoint) matches the described behavior, and the description is specific rather than keyword-baiting — it even enumerates exclusions. Security posture is unusually strong for a network-calling skill: explicit public-query acknowledgment gating, HTTPS-only base URLs with rejection of localhost/private/loopback/link-local addresses, rejection of cross-origin and protocol-downgrade redirects, no automatic fallback to alternate hosts, a 25 MiB response cap, no retry on POST, atomic 0600 artifact writes into a new/empty directory, strict regexes for CURIEs/categories/providers, and an explicit list of removed escape hatches (raw JSON submission, workflows, arbitrary operations, stdin lists, daemon/server/MCP surfaces). Epistemic guardrails discourage overclaiming results as clinical guidance. The only issues are minor: the referenced client script is absent so its controls cannot be verified, a residual DSL-interpolation surface for provider IDs (mitigated by allowlist), and the inherent disclosure of query terms to a third-party public service.

findings.title: Provider identifiers interpolated into ARAXi action strings
findings.description: The query contract states that user-supplied provider identifiers (`--kp`) are interpolated into an ARAXi DSL action sent to the remote ARAX service. String interpolation of user input into a remote DSL is an injection surface. The contract mitigates this with a strict allowlist regex (`^infores:[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$`), duplicate rejection, and a 2-5 provider cap, which appears adequate; the risk is residual and depends on the (absent) implementation actually enforcing the documented regex.
findings.snippet: Provider identifiers are interpolated into an ARAXi action and therefore use the stricter form: ^infores:[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$
findings.remediation: Ensure the implementation enforces the documented allowlist regex before interpolation and prefer structured/parameterized construction of the ARAXi action over string concatenation.

findings.title: Outbound transmission of user query terms to a third-party public service
findings.description: The skill sends biomedical entity names and CURIEs to the external production endpoint https://arax.transltr.io. This is the skill's stated purpose and is clearly disclosed. The manifest and instructions explicitly require an `--acknowledge-public-query` flag, warn that query and caller metadata may be publicly visible, prohibit patient or confidential data, and forbid placing user/project names in the submitter or User-Agent headers. No credentials, environment variables, or local files are collected or transmitted. Informational only.
findings.snippet: Every normalization or graph request requires --acknowledge-public-query. ... Never put a user name, project name, or query term into the submitter or User-Agent.
findings.remediation: No action required; retain the explicit public-query acknowledgment and the prohibition on sensitive content.

findings.description: offtarget_scan.py `contig` runs longest_common_substring() for every candidate against every transcript record loaded fully into memory by read_fasta(). scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The open-targets skill is a well-documented, read-only client for the public Open Targets Platform GraphQL API. All three Python scripts use only the standard library (urllib, json, csv, argparse) and contact a single, documented, unauthenticated public endpoint. There is no eval/exec/os.system usage, no subprocess invocation, no shell interpolation, no filesystem traversal, no credential or environment harvesting, no hardcoded secrets, no encoded or obfuscated payloads, and no third-party package installation. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; its instructions are purely domain guidance about identifier resolution and score interpretation. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) and the compatibility note explicitly disclosing outbound HTTPS access are consistent with observed behaviour, and the description — while keyword-rich — accurately and narrowly scopes the skill to Open Targets target–disease queries rather than inflating capability. Bundled reference files (references/graphql-schema.md, references/datasources.md, references/query-cookbook.md) are internal documentation containing only GraphQL examples with no embedded instructions to the agent; several additional referenced paths (assets/*, templates/*) are resolution artefacts and do not exist. Retry logic is bounded (max 4 attempts, capped 30s sleep) and the cursor-paging loop guards against repeated cursors, so there is no denial-of-service or infinite-loop risk. Only two minor, informational observations are noted: a configurable API endpoint and an arbitrary-GraphQL-document subcommand.

findings.title: GraphQL endpoint overridable via environment variable and CLI flag
findings.description: The shared transport module reads the API endpoint from the OPEN_TARGETS_API_URL environment variable and every CLI exposes an `--api-url` override. If an attacker can set that environment variable (or influence the command line), all GraphQL request bodies — including any user-supplied query text and variables passed through the `raw` subcommand — would be POSTed to an arbitrary host. This is a common, largely benign configurability pattern for public-API clients, but it is a theoretical redirection/exfiltration vector because there is no allow-list or scheme validation on the destination URL.
findings.snippet:
API_URL = os.environ.get("OPEN_TARGETS_API_URL", "https://api.platform.opentargets.org/api/v4/graphql")
...
parser.add_argument("--api-url", default=API_URL, help="override the GraphQL endpoint (default: the public Platform API)")
findings.remediation: Optionally validate that the endpoint uses HTTPS and, if practical, warn on stderr when a non-default host is used so redirection to an unexpected destination is visible to the user.

findings.title: `raw` subcommand executes arbitrary GraphQL documents from a local file path
findings.description: The `raw` subcommand reads any file path supplied on the command line and sends its contents as a GraphQL document, with `--var name=value` pairs parsed as JSON. This is intended functionality for a GraphQL client and cannot execute local code, but it does mean an agent could be induced (e.g., by a crafted .graphql file in a workspace) to issue queries beyond the documented subcommands. Impact is limited because the Open Targets API is read-only, unauthenticated, and public, and no local file contents other than the named query file are transmitted.
findings.snippet:
query = Path(args.query_file).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
...
emit(post(query, variables, url=args.api_url), output_format="json")
findings.remediation: No change strictly required; optionally document that the query file should be reviewed before execution and reject documents containing GraphQL mutations.

findings.title: API endpoint is overridable via environment variable and CLI flag, with API key auto-attached
findings.description: `_common.py` reads the API root from the `OPENFDA_API_URL` environment variable (and every script exposes a `--base-url` flag). `_build_url()` automatically appends the value of `OPENFDA_API_KEY` as a query parameter to whatever base URL is in effect. If an attacker or a poisoned environment sets `OPENFDA_API_URL` to a host they control, the user's openFDA API key would be transmitted to that host, and all query responses would come from an untrusted source. The default is the legitimate public endpoint (https://api.fda.gov) and the key in question is a free, low-value quota token, so real-world impact is minimal.
findings.snippet:
BASE_URL = os.environ.get("OPENFDA_API_URL", "https://api.fda.gov")
...
key = api_key()
if key:
    query.setdefault("api_key", key)
findings.remediation: Only attach `api_key` when the resolved base URL matches the official api.fda.gov host, and/or validate the scheme/host of any overridden base URL (require HTTPS and an allow-list).

findings.title: Unvalidated remote API text (label sections, boxed warnings) rendered directly into agent context
findings.description: `fda_labels.py` prints raw SPL section text and boxed-warning text fetched from the remote API straight to stdout, which is then read by the agent. Although openFDA is an authoritative government source and the content is public-domain regulatory text, any text returned by a remote service that is echoed into the model context is a theoretical indirect-prompt-injection surface (particularly if the base URL is overridden per the previous finding). No sanitisation or delimiting of remote text is performed.

for text in record.get(args.section) or []:
    collapsed = " ".join(str(text).split())
    ...
    print(textwrap.fill(row["text"][: args.chars], width=95))
findings.remediation: Clearly delimit or label remotely fetched text as untrusted data in the output, and instruct the agent in SKILL.md to treat API-returned label text as data, never as instructions.
